segments.t: Role of the NvM in the memory stack

The NVRAM manager (NvM) is the central service for non-volatile data of the Classic Platform. It exclusively provides implicit access: It copies blocks between NV memory and RAM, and the application works with the RAM data ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧. The environment shall access the non-volatile memory only via the NvM ⟦2⟧. Downwards, the NvM relies on the Memory Abstraction Interface (MemIf). Together with Flash EEPROM Emulation (Fee) or EEPROM Abstraction (Ea), it provides a virtual linear 32-bit address space ⟦3⟧. Upper layers only include ⟦4⟧ ⟦5⟧.

Depending on the configuration, the NvM receives the results of the lower layer in two ways. Either Fee/Ea call the callbacks ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧, or the NvM queries the job status in polling mode ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧. Both detection paths are also described by ⟦5⟧. Further neighboring modules:
Production errors go to the Dem ⟦0⟧.
Development errors go to the Det ⟦0⟧.
CRCs are calculated by the Crc module ⟦0⟧.
The NvM informs the BswM about multi-block and single-block states ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧.
Optionally, the NvM encrypts blocks via the Csm ⟦0⟧.
Context diagram: The NvM mediates between users and BswM on the one hand and MemIf/Fee/Ea on the other hand; Dem, Det, Crc and Csm are auxiliary services. Sources: ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧
NVRAM blocks: Structure and management types

Each NVRAM block consists of three mandatory components: NV block, RAM block and administrative block. A ROM block is optional ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧. The composition is determined by the block descriptor at configuration time ⟦2⟧. The components in detail:
The NV block contains user data and optionally CRC and header ⟦0⟧.
The ROM block provides default data for empty or corrupted NV blocks ⟦0⟧.
The administrative block is located in RAM and is invisible to the application. It holds the dataset index, attributes and error/status information ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧.

A block is addressed via its block ID ⟦0⟧. ⟦1⟧ is a ⟦2⟧; the dataset selection bits reduce its value range ⟦3⟧. Two IDs are reserved: 0 for the multi-block result and 1 for the configuration ID ⟦4⟧.

For DATASET blocks, ⟦0⟧ selects the element. Indexes from ⟦1⟧ onwards refer to ROM blocks ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧. The index is not stored persistently, and ⟦4⟧ sets it to zero. The user is responsible for the correct selection ⟦5⟧ ⟦6⟧ ⟦7⟧ (⟦8⟧).
Startup: NvM_Init and NvM_ReadAll

⟦0⟧ is exclusively called by the BswM ⟦1⟧. The configuration pointer is always ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧. The function resets the internal variables and signals "INIT DONE"; only after this does the NvM process jobs ⟦4⟧ ⟦5⟧. For time reasons, it neither initializes NVRAM blocks nor other modules, and it does not modify any permanent RAM blocks ⟦6⟧ ⟦7⟧ ⟦8⟧.

The data is subsequently loaded by the multi-block job ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧. The call only signals the job and returns immediately ⟦2⟧. It is only available in the NvM master ⟦3⟧. The job proceeds in the following steps:
First, it compares the stored configuration ID with the compiled one ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧.
If ⟦0⟧ is FALSE, it ignores a mismatch ⟦1⟧. Otherwise, the extended runtime preparation follows ⟦2⟧ (⟦3⟧).
Then it iterates over the user blocks ⟦0⟧. It only processes blocks with a permanent RAM block or explicit synchronization ⟦1⟧.
If a configured RAM CRC matches, the RAM content is considered valid ⟦0⟧. The single-block callback can be called per block ⟦1⟧. The overall result is ⟦2⟧, or ⟦3⟧ as soon as a block fails ⟦4⟧ ⟦5⟧.
The NvM reports the acceptance and completion of the job to the BswM ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧. The BswM then continues the startup, for instance with ⟦2⟧ (⟦3⟧; ⟦4⟧).
Sequence diagram: ⟦0⟧ only prepares the NvM; the block data is only loaded by the asynchronous ⟦1⟧, whose completion releases the further startup. Sources: ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧, ⟦5⟧, ⟦6⟧, ⟦7⟧
Single-block jobs: Queue, priority and feedback

Single-block services such as ⟦0⟧ or ⟦1⟧ operate asynchronously. They take over the parameters, queue the job and return ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧. After successful queuing, the result is set to ⟦5⟧ ⟦6⟧. If the queue overflows, the call returns ⟦7⟧ ⟦8⟧. A block is only queued if it is not already waiting or being processed ⟦9⟧.
The actual work happens in ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧. There, the NvM dequeues the highest priority job and processes the jobs sequentially ⟦2⟧. The following rules apply to the order:
With ⟦0⟧, the NvM uses two queues; one of them is for immediate write jobs (crash data) ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧.
Immediate jobs destructively interrupt running jobs; these are restarted afterwards ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧.
Without prioritization, the order of arrival applies ⟦0⟧.
⟦0⟧ is not interrupted. Read and write jobs arriving during a multi-block job are queued and executed afterwards ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧.

Which RAM buffer is used depends on the passed pointer. With ⟦0⟧, the NvM uses the permanent RAM block or explicit synchronization ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧. Another address serves as a temporary RAM block, even if a permanent one is configured ⟦5⟧ ⟦6⟧. For permanent RAM blocks, there are separate PRAM services ⟦7⟧ ⟦8⟧ (⟦9⟧).

The result is stored in the error/status field of the administrative block ⟦0⟧ and can be queried via ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧. If a single-block callback is configured, every job ends with its invocation from ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧ ⟦5⟧ ⟦6⟧. In addition, the BswM can be informed on a block-by-block basis ⟦7⟧ ⟦8⟧. ⟦9⟧ removes the waiting jobs of a block; an already running job is continued ⟦10⟧ ⟦11⟧.
Sequence diagram: The call returns immediately; the processing and the feedback via callback or status query follow in later ⟦0⟧ calls. Sources: ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧, ⟦5⟧, ⟦6⟧
RAM block state and synchronization with the application

The NvM maintains a "valid" or "invalid" state for the permanent RAM block or the mirror ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧. It additionally distinguishes valid blocks by changed and unchanged ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧. The transitions in detail:
Read and restore jobs invalidate the block upon queuing or job start ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧.
Successful reading results in "valid/unchanged" ⟦0⟧.
Loaded defaults result in "valid/changed" ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧. Without defaults, the block remains invalid ⟦2⟧.
⟦0⟧ with ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧ mark the block as changed ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧ (⟦5⟧).
After successful writing, the block is considered unchanged ⟦0⟧.

State diagram: Read and restore jobs temporarily invalidate the RAM block; only a write operation returns "changed" to "unchanged". The initial state is an interpretation. Sources: ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧, ⟦5⟧

With implicit synchronization, the NvM and the application access the same RAM block. After a read or write job, the application must therefore not use it again until the feedback ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧ (⟦2⟧). If several applications share a block, they are themselves responsible for its consistency ⟦3⟧.

Alternatively, ⟦0⟧ configures an explicit synchronization ⟦1⟧. The NvM then creates exactly one RAM mirror and uses it as a buffer ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧. The callbacks ⟦4⟧ and ⟦5⟧ copy between the application and the mirror ⟦6⟧ ⟦7⟧. Their signatures are ⟦8⟧ and ⟦9⟧ ⟦10⟧ ⟦11⟧. For this use case, they are mandatory entries (⟦12⟧).

Until the callback, the application may continue to modify its block ⟦0⟧ (⟦1⟧). If a callback reports ⟦2⟧, the NvM calls it again in the next run of the ⟦3⟧, at most ⟦4⟧ times ⟦5⟧ ⟦6⟧. A block with explicit synchronization must not have a permanent RAM block ⟦7⟧. The RTE implements these callbacks with an NvBlockSwComponent (⟦8⟧).

Sequence diagram: With explicit synchronization, the NvM only takes over the data in the mirror callback, thus delayed compared to the job; a failed callback is repeated. Sources: ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧, ⟦5⟧
Shutdown, protection mechanisms and configuration

The BswM triggers the shutdown with ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧. The call returns immediately and is only available in the NvM master ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧. The job writes permanent RAM blocks or calls the mirror callback ⟦4⟧ ⟦5⟧. Previously, it checks the "valid/changed" state ⟦6⟧. It skips write-protected and locked blocks without an error message ⟦7⟧ ⟦8⟧.

So that only changed blocks are written, the user reports changes via ⟦0⟧, provided this API is configured ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧. For ⟦3⟧, the RTE takes this over (⟦4⟧). ⟦5⟧ is reserved for the BswM ⟦6⟧. The currently processed block is completed consistently; the remaining blocks receive ⟦7⟧ ⟦8⟧ ⟦9⟧ ⟦10⟧ (⟦11⟧).
Sequence diagram: Changes reported at runtime are only written during ⟦0⟧; the BswM can cancel and waits for the result notification. Sources: ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧, ⟦5⟧
Further protection and configuration mechanisms at a glance:
Write protection: The write protection is a block attribute. With ⟦0⟧ it is active by default, and the environment can clear it with ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧.
Write once: Blocks with ⟦0⟧ are only written once. Their protection cannot be cleared, and write jobs before the first read are rejected ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧.
Lock: The lock via ⟦0⟧ cannot be changed by other services ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧.
Integrity: A static block ID in the header is stored when writing and checked when reading ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧. A CRC comparison can avoid writing unchanged data ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧.
Scope: There are three API configuration classes; class 1 does not support DATASET ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧.
First initialization: ⟦0⟧ writes defaults or invalidates blocks and ignores the write protection in the process ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧.
Development errors. When error detection is enabled, the NvM reports to the Det among other things:
For a full queue, ⟦0⟧ is additionally defined ⟦1⟧.
Read errors. The NvM controls the recovery itself (⟦0⟧). It proceeds step by step:
In case of CRC or static block ID errors, it reads again if necessary ⟦0⟧ ⟦1⟧.

For REDUNDANT blocks, it reads the second NV block ⟦0⟧. If one instance is valid, the result is ⟦1⟧, without a Dem report ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧. Afterwards, the NvM attempts to restore the redundancy; if this fails, it reports ⟦4⟧ ⟦5⟧ ⟦6⟧.
Otherwise, it loads defaults (⟦0⟧) without modifying the NV block ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧.
If there are no defaults, the RAM block remains invalid ⟦0⟧. The result then depends on the error type:
CRC error: ⟦0⟧ and Dem report ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧
Job error: ⟦0⟧ and Dem report ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧
An invalidated block results in ⟦0⟧ without a Dem entry ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧.
The ErrorDescription divergently names the result values ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ (⟦2⟧). However, the requirements ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧ are authoritative for R20-11.
Activity diagram: The read recovery goes through read retry, redundant copy and default data; only after this is an error set and reported to the Dem. Sources: ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧, ⟦5⟧, ⟦6⟧, ⟦7⟧

Write errors. Regardless of the management type, the NvM repeats failed write operations, at most ⟦0⟧ times ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧. Afterwards, it sets ⟦4⟧ and reports ⟦5⟧ ⟦6⟧ ⟦7⟧ (⟦8⟧). If the write verification fails, it reports ⟦9⟧ and repeats the writing ⟦10⟧ ⟦11⟧. For REDUNDANT blocks, one successfully written instance is sufficient for ⟦12⟧ ⟦13⟧. Checking erroneous data and providing valid data before the next writing is the responsibility of the application ⟦14⟧ ⟦15⟧.

System architecture and role of the module cluster

The cluster comprises a single module, the Runtime Environment (⟦0⟧). It implements the communication paths on each ECU that the ECU configuration specifies. In doing so, it also realizes the semantics of the communication attributes from the component descriptions ⟦1⟧ ⟦2⟧. The RTE is configured and generated individually for each ECU ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧. The generator produces C code which must comply with MISRA C ⟦5⟧ ⟦6⟧. The location of the RTE between application software and Basic Software is shown in the ECU architecture picture (⟦7⟧).

Downwards, the RTE exclusively uses standardized AUTOSAR services, including OS, COM, LdCom and Transformer ⟦0⟧. The generated code also includes the Basic Software Scheduler (SchM). It serves the scheduling, the modes, the triggers and the exclusive areas of the BSW modules. The methodology provides a separate generation step for this, which only generates the scheduler code (⟦1⟧).

The generator describes the generated RTE itself as a BSW module. This includes ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧ ⟦5⟧. The lifecycle APIs of Rte and SchM appear therein as ⟦6⟧ ⟦7⟧. Central interface files are:
